learn: What makes an LLM system an agent, and when to use one
Single-agent architecture: perception, memory, planning, tools
The ReAct loop as an agent controller
intro.why: Agents turn LLMs from answer generators into systems that carry out multi-step tasks: research, data analysis, coding, operations. They also introduce new risks that must be engineered around.

sections.title: From LLMs to agents
sections.plain: An agent is a model in a loop that chooses its own next actions and uses tools to reach a goal.
sections.body:
An LLM agent uses a language model to decide, step by step, which actions to take, executes them through tools, observes the results, and continues until the goal is met. Autonomy is a spectrum:

  1. Single LLM call.
  2. Fixed chains/workflows defined by developers.
  3. Routers that pick among predefined paths.
  4. Tool-using agent loops that choose actions dynamically.
  5. Multi-agent systems.

Agents suit open-ended tasks where the steps can't be fixed in advance (research, debugging, data exploration). They cost more, are slower and less predictable, so start with the simplest design that works and add autonomy only where it pays off.

sections.title: Single-agent architecture
sections.plain: An agent combines a model with the ability to perceive, remember, plan and act.
sections.body:
• Perception: what the agent can observe: user input, documents, tool outputs, web pages, images, screens.
  • Memory: short-term (the context window: conversation, scratchpad, recent observations) and long-term (external stores of facts, user preferences and past episodes, retrieved like RAG).
  • Planning: decomposing goals into sub-tasks, choosing order, re-planning after feedback (ReAct, plan-and-execute, reflection).
  • Tools / action: function calls to search, code execution, databases, APIs, browsers, file systems.

The control loop: perceive → reason → act → observe → update memory → repeat until finished or a limit is hit. Context management (summarising old steps, trimming tool outputs) is a practical necessity on long tasks.

sections.title: The ReAct loop
sections.plain: Think, use a tool, read the result, and repeat until you can answer.
sections.body:
The ReAct pattern (M11) is the standard agent controller: at each step the model writes a Thought, chooses an Action (tool and arguments), and receives an Observation; the trace becomes its working memory.

Worked (ex1): "What is double the population of France?" Step 1: search → about 68 million. Step 2: calculator[68 × 2] → 136. Step 3: finish → about 136 million. Each fact comes from a tool, and the loop is capped (max 5 steps) so it cannot run forever.

Modern APIs implement this with native function calling: the model returns tool calls, the application executes them and appends results, and the loop continues until the model returns a final message.

sections.title: Multi-agent systems
sections.plain: Several agents with different jobs work together, often coordinated by a manager agent.
sections.body:
Multi-agent systems split work among agents with different roles, prompts, tools or models. Patterns:

  • Orchestrator–workers: a planner decomposes the task and delegates sub-tasks (ex1: research → draft → check).
  • Critic / verifier: one agent reviews another's output.
  • Debate: agents argue positions; a judge decides.
  • Hand-offs: specialists pass the conversation along (triage → billing agent).

Benefits: specialisation, parallel exploration, separate context windows for sub-tasks. Costs: multiplied tokens and latency, coordination failures, and error cascades when one agent's mistake becomes another's premise. Use multiple agents when sub-tasks are genuinely separable.

sections.title: Text-to-SQL and data-frame agents
sections.plain: The agent writes database queries or analysis code, runs them safely, and explains the results.
sections.body:
Data agents translate questions into executable code: text-to-SQL against a database schema, or data-frame (pandas) code in a sandbox for analysis and charts. The loop: inspect schema → write query → validate → execute → read result or error → fix and retry → explain.

Worked (ex2): "Which city has the most revenue?" → SELECT city, SUM(amount) … ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 1 → Delhi, 350. "Average February order?" → 113.3. "Clean up old orders" → a DELETE, blocked by validation.

Safeguards: read-only credentials, statement allow-lists, row limits and timeouts, sandboxed code execution, and showing the query to the user. Schema descriptions and example queries improve accuracy.

sections.title: Agentic RAG
sections.plain: Let the agent decide what to search for, search again based on what it found, and stop when it has enough evidence.
sections.body:
Classic RAG retrieves once with the user's question. Agentic RAG puts retrieval under the agent's control: deciding whether to retrieve, rewriting queries, choosing sources (vector store, SQL, web), grading retrieved passages, and iterating for multi-hop questions.

Worked (ex2): "Who founded the company that makes the Model Q phone?" Search 1 → made by Orion Devices; search 2 (using that name) → founded by M. Iyer in 2009 (fictional example). A single retrieval with the original question would likely miss the second fact.

Benefits: better recall on complex questions and self-correction. Costs: more calls, latency, and more places for errors; keep iteration limits and cite every source used.

sections.title: Agent failure modes and safeguards
sections.plain: Agents can loop, misuse tools, pile up small errors or take harmful actions, so build in limits, checks and human approval.
sections.body:
Common failures: loops (repeating the same action), malformed or hallucinated tool calls, compounding errors (97% per-step reliability over 10 steps succeeds only ~74% of the time), context overflow, runaway cost, prompt injection via tool outputs or web pages, and unintended irreversible actions.

Safeguards:

  • Step, time and budget limits; loop detection (ex2 flags three identical actions).
  • Schema validation of tool arguments; least-privilege, sandboxed tools.
  • Human-in-the-loop approval for risky actions (sending email, payments, deletion).
  • Treat tool outputs as untrusted data; separate instructions from content.
  • Logging, tracing and evaluation on task suites; graceful failure messages.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Workflows often beat agents for well-understood processes: cheaper, testable, predictable.
  • Tool design matters as much as prompts: clear names, descriptions and error messages help the model use tools correctly.
  • Computer-use agents operate GUIs via screenshots and clicks, broadening reach and risk.
  • Evaluation needs end-to-end task success, not just per-step accuracy (M14).

code.title: A minimal agent and an orchestrator
code.explain: Runs a ReAct-style agent with search and a restricted calculator, short-term memory and a step limit (France ≈ 68 million → doubled → about 136 million in 3 steps), then an orchestrator that plans research → draft → check and delegates to worker functions, with a critic verifying claims.
code.notes: A rule-based policy stands in for the LLM so the trace is reproducible.
code.output:
step 1 | Thought: I need the current population first.
        | Action: search[population of France] -> Observation: about 68 million (2024 estimate)
step 2 | Thought: Double it.
        | Action: calculator[68 * 2] -> Observation: 136
step 3 | Thought: I have what I need.
        | Final answer: About 136 million.
[orchestrator] research key facts                  -> France ~68M people; capital Paris
[orchestrator] draft a 2-sentence summary          -> France has about 68 million people. Its capital is Paris.
[orchestrator] check the draft against the facts   -> OK: both claims supported

code.title: Text-to-SQL, agentic RAG and safeguards
code.explain: Validates and executes generated SQL on an in-memory database (Delhi 350; February average 113.3) while blocking a DELETE, answers a two-hop question by using the first search result to form the second query, detects a repeated-action loop, and routes risky tools to human approval.
mistakes: Giving agents write access to databases.
code.code:
"""Text-to-SQL with validation, an agentic multi-hop retrieval loop, and safeguards against loops and risky actions."""
import sqlite3, re

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER, city TEXT, amount REAL, month TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?,?,?,?)", [(1,"Pune",120,"Jan"),(2,"Delhi",300,"Jan"),(3,"Pune",80,"Feb"),(4,"Delhi",50,"Feb"),(5,"Chennai",210,"Feb")])
def validate(sql):
    s = sql.strip().lower()
    return s.startswith("select") and not re.search(r"\b(drop|delete|update|insert|alter)\b", s) and ";" not in s.rstrip(";")
for question, sql in [("Which city has the most revenue?", "SELECT city, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY city ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 1"),
                      ("Average February order?", "SELECT ROUND(AVG(amount), 1) FROM orders WHERE month = 'Feb'"),
                      ("Clean up old orders", "DELETE FROM orders WHERE month = 'Jan'")]:
    ok = validate(sql)
    res = db.execute(sql).fetchall() if ok else "blocked: only read-only SELECT queries are allowed"
    print(f"Q: {question}\n   SQL: {sql}\n   -> {res}")

# Agentic RAG: the second search depends on the first answer (multi-hop)
KB = {"maker of the Model Q phone": "The Model Q phone is made by Orion Devices.",
      "founder of Orion Devices": "Orion Devices was founded by M. Iyer in 2009."}
q = "Who founded the company that makes the Model Q phone?"
hop1 = KB["maker of the Model Q phone"]
company = re.search(r"made by ([A-Z][a-z]+ [A-Z][a-z]+)", hop1).group(1)
hop2 = KB[f"founder of {company}"]
print(f"\nagentic RAG for: {q}\n  search 1 -> {hop1}\n  search 2 (uses '{company}') -> {hop2}")
print("  a single retrieval with the original question would likely miss the second fact")

# Safeguards: step cap, repeated-action detection, human approval for risky tools
history = ["search[x]", "search[x]", "search[x]"]
print("\nloop detected:", len(history) >= 3 and len(set(history[-3:])) == 1)
RISKY = {"send_email", "transfer_money", "delete_file"}
for action in ("search", "send_email"):
    print(f"action {action}: {'needs human approval' if action in RISKY else 'allowed'}")
